The First Amendment guarantees the free exercise of religion in the country and forbids Congress from passing laws respecting its establishment.[480][481] Religious practice is widespread, among the most diverse in the world,[482] and profoundly vibrant.[483]

The country has the world's largest Christian population, which includes the fourth-largest population of Catholics.[484] Other notable faiths include Judaism, Buddhism, Hinduism, Islam, New Age, and Native American religions.[485] Religious practice varies significantly by region.[486] "Ceremonial deism" is common in American culture.[487]

The overwhelming majority of Americans believe in a higher power or spiritual force, engage in spiritual practices such as prayer, and consider themselves religious or spiritual.[488][489] In the Southern United States' "Bible Belt", evangelical Protestantism plays a significant role culturally; New England and the Western United States tend to be more secular.[486][490] Mormonism, a Restorationist movement founded in the U.S. in 1830,[491][492] is the predominant religion in Utah and a major religion in Idaho.

Health
Main article: Health in the United States
Further information: Healthcare in the United States and Health insurance in the United States
See also: History of public health in the United States and History of medicine in the United States
The Texas Medical Center in Houston is the largest medical complex in the world.[493][494] In 2018, it employed 120,000 people and treated 10 million patients.[495]

According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), average U.S. life expectancy at birth reached 79.0 years in 2024, its highest recorded level and an increase of 0.6 years over 2023. The CDC attributed the improvement mainly to lower mortality from unintentional injuries, COVID-19, heart disease, cancer, and homicide. Heart disease, cancer, and unintentional injuries remained the leading causes of death.[496] In 2024, life expectancy at birth for American men rose to 76.5 years (+0.7 years compared to 2023), while life expectancy for women was 81.4 years (+0.3 years).[497] Starting in 1998, life expectancy in the U.S. fell behind that of other wealthy industrialized countries, and Americans' "health disadvantage" gap has been increasing ever since.[498]

The Commonwealth Fund reported in 2020 that the U.S. had the highest suicide rate among the 11 high-income countries included in its study.[499] Obesity affected 40.3% of U.S. adults aged 20 and older in August 2021–August 2023.[500] The U.S. healthcare system far outspends that of any other country, measured both in per capita spending and as a percentage of GDP, but attains worse healthcare outcomes when compared to peer countries for reasons that are debated.[501] The United States is the only developed country without a system of universal healthcare, and a significant proportion of the population that does not carry health insurance.[502] Government-funded healthcare coverage for the poor (Medicaid) and for those age 65 and older (Medicare) is available to Americans who meet the programs' income or age qualifications. In 2010, President Barack Obama signed the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act into law.[y][503] Since the 2022 U.S. Supreme Court decision Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization, which effectively overruled Roe v. Wade (1973), abortion in the United States is no longer federally protected but is subject to the laws of each state or territory.[z][504]

Education
Main article: Education in the United States
Some 77% of American college students attend public institutions[505] such as the University of Virginia, founded by Thomas Jefferson in 1819.

American primary and secondary education, known in the U.S. as K–12 ("kindergarten through 12th grade"), is decentralized. School systems are operated by state, territorial, and sometimes municipal governments and regulated by the U.S. Department of Education. In general, children are required to attend school or an approved homeschool from the age of five or six (kindergarten or first grade) until they are 18 years old. This often brings students through the 12th grade, the final year of a U.S. high school, but some states and territories allow them to leave school earlier, at age 16 or 17.[506] The U.S. spends more on education per student than any other country,[507] an average of $18,614 per year per public elementary and secondary school student in 2020–2021.[508] Among Americans age 25 and older, 92.2% graduated from high school, 62.7% attended some college, 37.7% earned a bachelor's degree, and 14.2% earned a graduate degree.[509] The U.S. literacy rate is near-universal.[365][510] The U.S. has produced the most Nobel Prize winners of any country, with 411 (having won 413 awards).[511][512]

U.S. tertiary or higher education has earned a global reputation. Many of the world's top universities, as listed by various ranking organizations, are in the United States, including 19 of the top 25.[513][514] American higher education is dominated by state university systems, although the country's many private universities and colleges enroll about 20% of all American students. Local community colleges generally offer open admissions, lower tuition, and coursework leading to an associate degree or a non-degree certificate.[515]

As for public expenditures on higher education, the U.S. spends more per student than the OECD average, and Americans spend more than all nations in combined public and private spending.[516] Colleges and universities directly funded by the federal government do not charge tuition and are limited to military personnel and government employees, including: the U.S. service academies, the Naval Postgraduate School, and military staff colleges. Despite some student loan forgiveness programs in place,[517] student loan debt increased by 102% between 2010 and 2020,[518] and exceeded $1.7 trillion in 2022.[519]

Culture and society
Main articles: Culture of the United States and Society of the United States
See also: Human rights in the United States
The Statue of Liberty (Liberty Enlightening the World) on Liberty Island in New York Harbor was an 1886 gift from France that has become an iconic symbol of the American Dream.[520]

The United States is home to a wide variety of ethnic groups, traditions, and customs.[521][522] The country has been described as having the values of individualism and personal autonomy,[523][524] as well as a strong work ethic[525] and competitiveness.[526] Voluntary altruism toward others also plays a major role;[527][528][529] according to a 2016 study by the Charities Aid Foundation, Americans donated 1.44% of total GDP to charity—the highest rate in the world by a large margin.[530] Americans have traditionally been characterized by a unifying political belief in an "American Creed" that emphasizes consent of the governed, liberty, equality under the law, democracy, social equality, property rights, and a preference for limited government.[aa][531][532] The U.S. has acquired significant hard and soft power through its diplomatic influence, economic power, military alliances, and cultural exports such as American movies, music, video games, sports, and food.[533][534] The influence that the United States exerts on other countries through soft power is referred to as Americanization.[535]

Nearly all present Americans or their ancestors came from Europe, Africa, or Asia (the "Old World") within the past five centuries.[536] Mainstream American culture is a Western culture largely derived from the traditions of European immigrants with influences from many other sources, such as traditions brought by slaves from Africa.[537][538] More recent immigration from Asia and especially Latin America has added to a cultural mix that has been described as a homogenizing melting pot, and a heterogeneous salad bowl, with immigrants contributing to, and often assimilating into, mainstream American culture.

Under the First Amendment to the Constitution, the United States is considered to have the strongest protections of free speech of any country.[539] Flag desecration, hate speech, blasphemy, and lese majesty are all forms of protected expression.[540][541][542] A 2016 Pew Research Center poll found that Americans were the most supportive of free expression of any polity measured.[543] Additionally, they are the "most supportive of freedom of the press and the right to use the Internet without government censorship".[544] The U.S. is a socially progressive country[545] with permissive attitudes surrounding human sexuality.[546] LGBTQ rights in the United States are among the most advanced by global standards.[546][547][548]

The American Dream, or the perception that Americans enjoy high levels of social mobility, plays a key role in attracting immigrants.[549][550] Whether this perception is accurate has been a topic of debate.[551][552][553] While mainstream culture holds that the United States is a classless society,[554] scholars identify significant differences between the country's social classes, affecting socialization, language, and values.[555][556] Americans tend to greatly value socioeconomic achievement, but being ordinary or average is promoted by some as a noble condition as well.[557]

The National Foundation on the Arts and the Humanities is an agency of the United States federal government that was established in 1965 with the purpose to "develop and promote a broadly conceived national policy of support for the humanities and the arts in the United States, and for institutions which preserve the cultural heritage of the United States."[558]

Literature
Main article: American literature
See also: American philosophy
Mark Twain, whom William Faulkner called "the father of American literature"[559]

Colonial American authors were influenced by John Locke and other Enlightenment philosophers.[560][561] The American Revolutionary Period (1765–1783) is notable for the political writings of Benjamin Franklin, Alexander Hamilton, Thomas Paine, and Thomas Jefferson. Shortly before and after the Revolutionary War, the newspaper rose to prominence, filling a demand for anti-British national literature.[562][563] An early novel is William Hill Brown's The Power of Sympathy, published in 1789.[564] Writer and critic John Neal in the early- to mid-19th century helped advance America toward a unique literature and culture by criticizing predecessors such as Washington Irving for imitating their British counterparts, and by influencing writers such as Edgar Allan Poe,[565] who took American poetry and short fiction in new directions. Ralph Waldo Emerson and Margaret Fuller pioneered the influential Transcendentalism movement;[566][567] Henry David Thoreau, author of Walden, was influenced by this movement.

The conflict surrounding abolitionism inspired writers, like Harriet Beecher Stowe, and authors of slave narratives, such as Frederick Douglass. Nathaniel Hawthorne's The Scarlet Letter (1850) explored the dark side of American history, as did Herman Melville's Moby-Dick (1851). Major American poets of the 19th century American Renaissance include Walt Whitman, Melville, and Emily Dickinson.[568][569] Mark Twain was the first major American writer to be born in the West. Henry James achieved international recognition with novels like The Portrait of a Lady (1881). As literacy rates rose, periodicals published more stories centered around industrial workers, women, and the rural poor.[570][571] Naturalism, regionalism, and realism were the major literary movements of the period.[572][573]

While modernism generally took on an international character, modernist authors working within the United States more often rooted their work in specific regions, peoples, and cultures.[574] Following the Great Migration to northern cities, African-American and black West Indian authors of the Harlem Renaissance developed an independent tradition of literature that rebuked a history of inequality and celebrated black culture. An important cultural export during the Jazz Age, these writings were a key influence on Négritude, a philosophy emerging in the 1930s among francophone writers of the African diaspora.[575][576] In the 1950s, an ideal of homogeneity led many authors to attempt to write the Great American Novel,[577] while the Beat Generation rejected this conformity, using styles that elevated the impact of the spoken word over mechanics to describe drug use, sexuality, and the failings of society.[578][579] Contemporary literature is more pluralistic than in previous eras, with the closest thing to a unifying feature being a trend toward self-conscious experiments with language.[580] Twelve American laureates have won the Nobel Prize in Literature.[581]

Mass media
Main article: Mass media in the United States
See also: Newspapers in the United States, Television in the United States, Broadcasting in the United States, Public broadcasting in the United States, Internet in the United States, Radio in the United States, and Video games in the United States
Comcast Center in Philadelphia, headquarters of Comcast, one of the world's largest telecommunications companies and media conglomerates

The four major broadcasters in the U.S. are the National Broadcasting Company (NBC), Columbia Broadcasting System (CBS), American Broadcasting Company (ABC), and Fox Broadcasting Company (Fox). The four major broadcast television networks are all commercial entities. The Public Broadcasting Service (PBS) is the country's major non-commercial public broadcast network;[582] it also provides educational programming through local PBS stations.[583][584][585][586] The U.S. cable television system offers hundreds of channels catering to a variety of niches.[587] In 2021, about 83% of Americans over age 12 listened to broadcast radio, while about 40% listened to podcasts.[588] In the prior year, there were 15,460 licensed full-power radio stations in the U.S. according to the Federal Communications Commission (FCC).[589] Public radio broadcasting is largely supplied by National Public Radio (NPR), incorporated in February 1970 under the Public Broadcasting Act of 1967.[590]

U.S. newspapers with a global reach and reputation include The Wall Street Journal, The New York Times, The Washington Post, and USA Today.[591] About 800 publications are produced in Spanish.[592][593] With few exceptions, newspapers are privately owned, either by large chains such as Gannett or McClatchy, which own dozens or even hundreds of newspapers; by small chains that own a handful of papers; or, in an increasingly rare situation, by individuals or families. Major cities often have alternative newspapers to complement the mainstream daily papers, such as The Village Voice in New York City and LA Weekly in Los Angeles. The five most-visited websites in the world are Google, YouTube, Facebook, Instagram, and ChatGPT—all of them American-owned. Other popular platforms used include X (formerly Twitter) and Amazon.[594][595] In 2025, the U.S. was the world's second-largest video game market by revenue (after China).[596] In 2015, the U.S. video game industry consisted of 2,457 companies that employed around 220,000 jobs and generated $30.4 billion in revenue.[597] There are 444 game publishers, developers, and hardware companies in California alone.[598] In the Game Developers Conference (GDC) 2025 survey, 58% of responding game developers were based in the U.S.[599]

Media freedom was classified as "problematic" by Reporters Without Borders in 2026, and scholars have noted a significant rise in censorship and self-censorship in recent years.[600]

Theater
Main article: Theater in the United States
Broadway theaters in Theater District, Manhattan

The United States is well known for its theater. Mainstream theater in the United States derives from the old European theatrical tradition and has been heavily influenced by the British theater.[601] By the middle of the 19th century, America had created new distinct dramatic forms in the Tom Shows, the showboat theater and the minstrel show.[602] The central hub of the American theater scene is the Theater District in Manhattan, with its divisions of Broadway, off-Broadway, and off-off-Broadway.[603]

Many movie and television celebrities have gotten their big break working in New York productions. Outside New York City, many cities have professional regional or resident theater companies that produce their own seasons. The biggest-budget theatrical productions are musicals. U.S. theater has an active community theater culture.[604]

The Tony Awards recognize excellence in live Broadway theater and are presented at an annual ceremony in Manhattan. The awards are given for Broadway productions and performances. One is also given for regional theater.[605]

Visual arts
Main articles: Visual art of the United States and Architecture of the United States
American Gothic (1930) by Grant Wood is one of the most famous American paintings and is widely parodied.[606]

Folk art in colonial America grew out of artisanal craftsmanship in communities that allowed commonly trained people to individually express themselves. It was distinct from Europe's tradition of high art, which was less accessible and generally less relevant to early American settlers.[607] Cultural movements in art and craftsmanship in colonial America generally lagged behind those of Western Europe. For example, the prevailing medieval style of woodworking and primitive sculpture became integral to early American folk art, despite the emergence of Renaissance styles in England in the late 16th and early 17th centuries. The new English styles would have been early enough to make a considerable impact on American folk art, but American styles and forms had already been firmly adopted. Not only did styles change slowly in early America, but there was a tendency for rural artisans there to continue their traditional forms longer than their urban counterparts did—and far longer than those in Western Europe.[539]

The Hudson River School was a mid-19th-century movement in the visual arts tradition of European naturalism. The 1913 Armory Show in New York City, an exhibition of European modernist art, shocked the public and transformed the U.S. art scene.[608]

American Realism and American Regionalism sought to reflect and give America new ways of looking at itself. Georgia O'Keeffe, Marsden Hartley, and others experimented with new and individualistic styles, which would become known as American modernism. Major artistic movements such as the abstract expressionism of Jackson Pollock and Willem de Kooning and the pop art of Andy Warhol and Roy Lichtenstein developed largely in the United States. Major photographers include Alfred Stieglitz, Edward Steichen, Dorothea Lange, Edward Weston, James Van Der Zee, Ansel Adams, and Gordon Parks.[609]

The tide of modernism and then postmodernism has brought global fame to American architects, including Frank Lloyd Wright, Philip Johnson, and Frank Gehry.[610] The Metropolitan Museum of Art in Manhattan is the largest art museum in the United States[611] and the fourth-largest in the world.[612]

Music
Main article: Music of the United States
The Country Music Hall of Fame and Museum in Nashville, Tennessee

American folk music encompasses numerous music genres, variously known as traditional music, traditional folk music, contemporary folk music, or roots music. Many traditional songs have been sung within the same family or folk group for generations, and sometimes trace back to such origins as the British Isles, mainland Europe, or Africa.[613] The rhythmic and lyrical styles of African-American music in particular have influenced American music.[614] Banjos were brought to America through the slave trade. Minstrel shows incorporating the instrument into their acts led to its increased popularity and widespread production in the 19th century.[615][616] The electric guitar, first invented in the 1930s, and mass-produced by the 1940s, had an enormous influence on popular music, in particular due to the development of rock and roll.[617] The synthesizer, turntablism, and electronic music were also largely developed in the U.S.

Elements from folk idioms such as the blues and old-time music were adopted and transformed into popular genres with global audiences. Jazz grew from blues and ragtime in the early 20th century, developing from the innovations and recordings of composers such as W.C. Handy and Jelly Roll Morton. Louis Armstrong and Duke Ellington increased its popularity early in the 20th century.[618] Country music developed in the 1920s,[619] bluegrass[620] and rhythm and blues in the 1940s,[621] and rock and roll in the 1950s.[617] In the 1960s, Bob Dylan emerged from the folk revival to become one of the country's most celebrated songwriters.[622] The musical forms of punk and hip hop both originated in the United States in the 1970s.[623]

The United States has the world's largest music market, with a total retail value of $15.9 billion in 2022,[624] and is the largest exporter of music.[625][626] Most of the world's major record companies are based in the U.S.; they are represented by the Recording Industry Association of America (RIAA).[627] Mid-20th-century American pop stars, such as Frank Sinatra[628] and Elvis Presley,[629] became global celebrities and best-selling music artists,[618] as have artists of the late 20th century, such as Michael Jackson,[630] Madonna,[631] Whitney Houston,[632] and Mariah Carey,[633] and of the early 21st century, such as Eminem,[634] Britney Spears,[635] Lady Gaga,[635] Katy Perry,[635] Taylor Swift and Beyoncé.[636]

Fashion
Main article: Fashion in the United States
Haute couture fashion models on the catwalk during New York Fashion Week

The United States has the world's largest apparel market by revenue.[637] Apart from professional business attire, American fashion is eclectic and predominantly informal. Americans' diverse cultural roots are reflected in their clothing; however, sneakers, jeans, T-shirts, and baseball caps are emblematic of American styles.[638] New York, with its Fashion Week, is considered to be one of the "Big Four" global fashion capitals, along with Paris, Milan, and London. A study demonstrated that general proximity to Manhattan's Garment District has been synonymous with American fashion since its inception in the early 20th century.[639]

A number of well-known designer labels, among them Tommy Hilfiger, Ralph Lauren, Tom Ford and Calvin Klein, are headquartered in Manhattan.[640][641] Labels cater to niche markets, such as preteens. New York Fashion Week is one of the most influential fashion shows in the world, and is held twice each year in Manhattan;[642] the annual Met Gala, also in Manhattan, has been called the fashion world's "biggest night".[643][644]

Cinema
Main article: Cinema of the United States
The Hollywood Sign in the Hollywood Hills, often regarded as the symbol of the American film industry

The U.S. film industry has a worldwide influence and following. Hollywood, a district in central Los Angeles, the nation's second-most populous city, is also metonymous for the American filmmaking industry.[645][646][647] The major film studios of the United States are the primary source of the most commercially successful movies selling the most tickets in the world.[648][649]

Largely centered in the New York City region from its beginnings in the late 19th century through the first decades of the 20th century,[650][651][652][653] the U.S. film industry has since been primarily based in and around Hollywood. Nonetheless, American film companies have been subject to the forces of globalization in the 21st century, and an increasing number of films are made elsewhere.[654] The Academy Awards, popularly known as "the Oscars", have been held annually by the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences since 1929,[655] and the Golden Globes have been held annually since January 1944.[656]

The industry peaked in what is commonly referred to as the "Golden Age of Hollywood", from the early sound period until the early 1960s,[657] with screen actors such as John Wayne and Marilyn Monroe becoming iconic figures.[658][659] In the 1970s, "New Hollywood", or the "Hollywood Renaissance",[660] was defined by grittier films influenced by French and Italian realist pictures of the post-war period.[661] The 21st century has been marked by the rise of American streaming platforms, which came to rival traditional cinema.[662][663]

Cuisine
Main article: American cuisine
A Thanksgiving dinner with roast turkey, mashed potatoes, pickles, corn, candied yams, cranberry jelly, shrimps, stuffing, green peas, deviled eggs, green salad, and apple sauce

Early settlers were introduced by Native Americans to foods such as turkey, sweet potatoes, corn, squash, and maple syrup. Of the most enduring and pervasive examples are variations of the native dish called succotash. Early settlers and later immigrants combined these with foods they were familiar with, such as wheat flour,[664] beef, and milk, to create a distinctive American cuisine.[665][666] New World crops, especially pumpkin, corn, potatoes, and turkey as the main course are part of a shared national menu on Thanksgiving, when many Americans prepare or purchase traditional dishes to celebrate the occasion.[667]

Characteristic American dishes such as apple pie, fried chicken, doughnuts, french fries, macaroni and cheese, ice cream, hamburgers, hot dogs, and American pizza derive from the recipes of various immigrant groups.[668][669][670][671] Mexican dishes such as burritos and tacos preexisted the United States in areas later annexed from Mexico, and adaptations of Chinese cuisine as well as pasta dishes freely adapted from Italian sources are all widely consumed.[672]

American chefs have had a significant impact on society both domestically and internationally. In 1946, the Culinary Institute of America was founded by Katharine Angell and Frances Roth. This would become the United States' most prestigious culinary school, where many of the most talented American chefs would study prior to successful careers.[673][674] The United States restaurant industry was projected at $899 billion in sales for 2020,[675][676] and employed more than 15 million people, representing 10% of the nation's workforce directly.[675] It is the country's second-largest private employer and the third-largest employer overall.[677][678] The United States is home to over 220 Michelin-starred restaurants, 14 of which were awarded three stars.[679]

Wine has been produced in what is now the United States since the 1500s, with the first widespread production beginning in what is now New Mexico in 1628.[680][681][682] In the modern U.S., wine production is undertaken in all fifty states, with California producing 84 percent of all U.S. wine. With more than 1,100,000 acres (4,500 km2) under vine, the United States is the fourth-largest wine-producing country in the world, after Italy, Spain, and France.[683][684]

The classic American diner, a casual restaurant type originally intended for the working class, emerged during the 19th century from converted railroad dining cars made stationary. The diner soon evolved into purpose-built structures whose number expanded greatly in the 20th century.[685] The American fast-food industry developed alongside the nation's car culture.[686] American restaurants developed the drive-in format in the 1920s, which they began to replace with the drive-through format by the 1940s.[687][688] American fast-food restaurant chains, such as McDonald's, Burger King, Chick-fil-A, Kentucky Fried Chicken, Dunkin' Donuts and many others, have numerous outlets around the world.[689]

Sports
Main articles: Sports in the United States and United States at the Olympics
A collegiate-level game of American football, the most popular sport in the U.S.

The most popular spectator sports in the U.S. are American football, basketball, baseball, soccer, and ice hockey.[690] Their premier leagues are, respectively, the National Football League, National Basketball Association, Major League Baseball, Major League Soccer, and the National Hockey League.[691][692][693][694] All these leagues, excluding soccer, are considered to be preeminent in their respective sports worldwide.

While most major U.S. sports such as baseball and American football have evolved out of European practices, basketball, volleyball, skateboarding, and snowboarding are American inventions, many of which have become popular worldwide.[695] Lacrosse and surfing arose from Native American and Native Hawaiian activities that predate European contact.[696] The U.S. professional sports market was approximately $69 billion in July 2013, roughly 50% larger than that of Europe, the Middle East, and Africa combined.[697] Professional wrestling was widely popularized in the country, with the United States serving as the home country for World Wrestling Entertainment and All Elite Wrestling, the two largest wrestling promotions in the world.

American football is by several measures the most popular spectator sport in the United States.[698] Though American football does not have a substantial following in other nations, the NFL has the highest average attendance (67,254)[699] of any professional sports league in the world, and generated over $23 billion in revenue in the 2024 financial year.[700] Baseball has been regarded as the U.S. "national sport" since the late 19th century. The most-watched individual sports in the U.S. are golf and auto racing, particularly NASCAR and IndyCar.[701][702]

On the collegiate level, the NCAA reported $1.1 billion in revenue for the 2017 fiscal year,[703] and college football and basketball attract large audiences, as the NCAA March Madness tournament and the College Football Playoff are some of the most watched national sporting events.[704] In the U.S., the intercollegiate sports level serves as the main feeder system for professional and Olympic sports, with significant exceptions such as Minor League Baseball. This differs greatly from practices in nearly all other countries, where publicly and privately funded sports organizations serve this function.[705]

Eight Olympic Games have taken place in the United States, beginning with the 1904 Summer Olympics in St. Louis, Missouri.[706] The U.S. is scheduled to host the 2028 Summer Olympics in Los Angeles and the 2034 Winter Olympics in Salt Lake City. U.S. athletes have won a total of 2,968 medals (1,179 gold) at the Olympic Games, the most of any country.[707][708][709]

In other international competition, the United States is the home of a number of prestigious events, including the America's Cup, World Baseball Classic, the U.S. Open, and the Masters Tournament. The U.S. men's national soccer team has qualified for eleven World Cups, while the women's national team has won the FIFA Women's World Cup and Olympic soccer tournament four and five times, respectively.[710] The 1999 FIFA Women's World Cup was hosted by the United States. Its final match was attended by 90,185, setting the world record for largest women's sporting event crowd at the time.[711] The United States hosted the 1994 FIFA World Cup and co-hosted, along with Canada and Mexico, the 2026 FIFA World Cup.[712]

**William Bradford Shockley** (February 13, 1910 – August 12, 1989) was an American [physicist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physicist "Physicist"). He was the manager of a research group at [Bell Labs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bell_Labs "Bell Labs") that included [John Bardeen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Bardeen "John Bardeen") and [Walter Brattain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Brattain "Walter Brattain"). The three scientists were jointly awarded the 1956 [Nobel Prize in Physics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physics "Nobel Prize in Physics") "for their researches on [semiconductors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semiconductor "Semiconductor") and their discovery of the [transistor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transistor "Transistor") effect."[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-Nobel_Prize-2)

Partly as a result of Shockley's attempts to commercialize a new transistor design in the 1950s and 1960s, California's [Silicon Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon_Valley "Silicon Valley") became a hotbed of electronics innovation. He recruited brilliant employees, but quickly alienated them with his autocratic and erratic management; they left and founded major companies in the industry.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-MM18-3)

In his later life, while he was a professor of electrical engineering at [Stanford University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University "Stanford University") and afterward, Shockley became known for his outspoken promotion of [racism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racism "Racism") and [eugenics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eugenics "Eugenics").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-10)

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=William_Shockley&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

William Bradford Shockley was born on February 13, 1910, in [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London") to American parents, and was raised in the family's hometown of [Palo Alto, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palo_Alto,_California "Palo Alto, California"), from the age of three. [[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-IREProceedings1952-11) His father, [William Hillman Shockley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Hillman_Shockley "William Hillman Shockley"), was a mining engineer who speculated in mines for a living and spoke eight languages. His mother, [May Bradford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/May_Bradford "May Bradford"), grew up in the American West, graduated from [Stanford University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University "Stanford University"), and became the first female U.S. deputy mining surveyor.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-Shurkin2006p3-12)

Shockley was homeschooled up to the age of eight, due to his parents' dislike of public schools as well as Shockley's habit of violent tantrums.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-13) Shockley learned some physics at a young age from a neighbor who was a Stanford physics professor.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-14) Shockley spent two years at [Palo Alto Military Academy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harker_School "Harker School"), then briefly enrolled in the Los Angeles Coaching School to study physics and later graduated from [Hollywood High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hollywood_High_School "Hollywood High School") in 1927.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-:1-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-16)

Shockley obtained a [B.S.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B.S. "B.S.") from the [California Institute of Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_Institute_of_Technology "California Institute of Technology") in 1932. He then entered the [Massachusetts Institute of Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Institute_of_Technology "Massachusetts Institute of Technology"), where he received his [Ph.D.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ph.D. "Ph.D.") in 1936 with a thesis on the [electronic band structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronic_band_structure "Electronic band structure") of [sodium chloride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sodium_chloride "Sodium chloride").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-Shurkin2006pp38%E2%80%9339-17)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-thesis-1)

## Career and research

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=William_Shockley&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career and research")]

Shockley was one of the first recruits to [Bell Telephone Laboratories](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bell_Telephone_Laboratories "Bell Telephone Laboratories") by [Mervin Kelly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mervin_Kelly "Mervin Kelly"), who became director of research at the company in 1936 and focused on hiring [solid-state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solid-state_physics "Solid-state physics") physicists.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-:5-18) Shockley joined a group headed by [Clinton Davisson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clinton_Davisson "Clinton Davisson") in [Murray Hill, New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murray_Hill,_New_Jersey "Murray Hill, New Jersey").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-19) Executives at Bell Labs had theorized that [semiconductors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semiconductors "Semiconductors") may offer solid-state alternatives to the [vacuum tubes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vacuum_tube "Vacuum tube") used throughout Bell's nationwide telephone system. Shockley conceived a number of designs based on copper-oxide semiconductor materials, and collaborated with [Walter Brattain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Brattain "Walter Brattain")'s unsuccessful attempt to create a prototype in 1939.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-:5-18)

Shockley published a number of fundamental papers on solid-state physics in _[Physical Review](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physical\_Review "Physical Review")_. In 1938, he received his first patent, "Electron Discharge Device", on [electron multipliers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electron_multiplier "Electron multiplier").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-Shurkin2006p48-20)

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4a/William_Shockley_-_U.S._Army_maps_%28Bp463by2692%29.jpg/250px-William_Shockley_-_U.S._Army_maps_%28Bp463by2692%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:William_Shockley_-_U.S._Army_maps_(Bp463by2692).jpg)

Shockley (left) during his years in military research

During [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"), Shockley's prior research was interrupted and he became involved in [radar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radar "Radar") research in [Manhattan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhattan "Manhattan") ([New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City")). Also at Bell, early in 1942 Shockley pioneered applied work on [Delay-line memory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delay-line_memory "Delay-line memory"), which was 1/100th the cost of competing electronic memory of [vacuum tube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vacuum_tube "Vacuum tube") technology and approximately as rapid.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-21) This technology was incorporated inside the [ENIAC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ENIAC "ENIAC") computer by 1945.

In May 1942, he took leave from Bell Labs to become a research director at [Columbia University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_University "Columbia University")'s Anti-Submarine Warfare Operations Group.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-22) This involved devising methods for countering the tactics of submarines with improved [convoying](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convoy "Convoy") techniques, optimizing [depth charge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Depth_charge "Depth charge") patterns, and so on. Shockley traveled frequently to [the Pentagon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pentagon "The Pentagon") and Washington to meet high-ranking officers and government officials.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-23)

In 1944, he organized a training program for [B-29](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B-29 "B-29") bomber pilots to use new [radar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radar "Radar") bomb sights. In late 1944, he took a three-month tour to bases around the world to assess the results. For this project, Secretary of War [Robert Patterson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Porter_Patterson "Robert Porter Patterson") awarded Shockley the [Medal for Merit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medal_for_Merit "Medal for Merit") on October 17, 1946.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-Shurkin2006p85-24) In July 1945, the [War Department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_War "United States Department of War") asked Shockley to prepare a report on the question of probable casualties from an invasion of the Japanese mainland. Shockley concluded:

> If the study shows that the behavior of nations in all historical cases comparable to Japan's has in fact been invariably consistent with the behavior of the troops in battle, then it means that the Japanese dead and ineffectives at the time of the defeat will exceed the corresponding number for the Germans. In other words, we shall probably have to kill at least 5 to 10 million Japanese. This might cost us between 1.7 and 4 million casualties including 400,000 to 800,000 killed.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-Giangreco1997-25)

This report influenced the decision of the United States to drop [atomic bombs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_bombings_of_Hiroshima_and_Nagasaki "Atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki") on Hiroshima and Nagasaki, which preceded the surrender of Japan.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-26)

Shockley was the first physicist to propose a [log-normal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Log-normal_distribution "Log-normal distribution") distribution to model the creation process for scientific research papers.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-27)

### Invention of the transistor

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=William_Shockley&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Invention of the transistor")]

See also: [History of the transistor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_transistor "History of the transistor")

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c2/Bardeen_Shockley_Brattain_1948.JPG/250px-Bardeen_Shockley_Brattain_1948.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bardeen_Shockley_Brattain_1948.JPG)

[John Bardeen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Bardeen "John Bardeen"), Shockley _(center)_, and [Walter Brattain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Brattain "Walter Brattain") at Bell Labs, 1948

Shortly after the war ended in 1945, Bell Labs formed a solid-state physics group, led by Shockley and chemist Stanley Morgan, which included [John Bardeen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Bardeen "John Bardeen"), [Walter Brattain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Brattain "Walter Brattain"), physicist [Gerald Pearson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerald_Pearson "Gerald Pearson"), chemist Robert Gibney, electronics expert Hilbert Moore, and several technicians. Their assignment was to seek a solid-state alternative to fragile glass [vacuum tube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vacuum_tube "Vacuum tube") amplifiers. First attempts were based on Shockley's ideas about using an external electrical field on a semiconductor to affect its conductivity. These experiments failed every time in all sorts of configurations and materials. The group was at a standstill until Bardeen suggested a theory that invoked [surface states](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface_states "Surface states") that prevented the field from penetrating the semiconductor. The group changed its focus to study these surface states and they met almost daily to discuss the work. The group had excellent rapport and freely exchanged ideas.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-28)

By the winter of 1946, they had enough results that Bardeen submitted a paper on the surface states to _Physical Review_. Brattain started experiments to study the surface states through observations made while shining a bright light on the semiconductor's surface. This led to several more papers (one of them co-authored with Shockley), which estimated the density of the surface states to be more than enough to account for their failed experiments. The pace of the work picked up significantly when they started to surround point contacts between the semiconductor and the conducting wires with [electrolytes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrolyte "Electrolyte"). Moore built a circuit that allowed them to vary the frequency of the input signal easily. Finally they began to get some evidence of power amplification when Pearson, acting on a suggestion by Shockley, put a voltage on a droplet of glycol borate placed across a [p–n junction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%E2%80%93n_junction "P–n junction").[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-Crystal_Fire_p._132-29)

Bell Labs' attorneys soon discovered Shockley's field effect principle had been anticipated and devices based on it patented in 1930 by [Julius Lilienfeld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Lilienfeld "Julius Lilienfeld"), who filed his [MESFET](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MESFET "MESFET")-like patent in Canada on October 22, 1925.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-30)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-31) Although the patent appeared "breakable" (it could not work) the patent attorneys based one of its four patent applications only on the Bardeen-Brattain point contact design. Three others (submitted first) covered the electrolyte-based transistors with Bardeen, Gibney and Brattain as the inventors.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Shockley's name was not on any of these patent applications. This angered Shockley, who thought his name should also be on the patents because the work was based on his field effect idea. He even made efforts to have the patent written only in his name, and told Bardeen and Brattain of his intentions.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-32)

Shockley, angered by not being included on the patent applications, secretly continued his own work to build a different sort of transistor based on junctions instead of point contacts; he expected this kind of design would be more likely to be commercially viable. The point contact transistor, he believed, would prove to be fragile and difficult to manufacture. Shockley was also dissatisfied with certain parts of the explanation for how the point contact transistor worked and conceived of the possibility of [minority carrier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minority_carrier "Minority carrier") injection.

On February 13, 1948, another team member, [John N. Shive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_N._Shive "John N. Shive"), built a point contact transistor with bronze contacts on the front and back of a thin wedge of [germanium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germanium "Germanium"), proving that [holes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electron_hole "Electron hole") could diffuse through bulk germanium and not just along the surface as previously thought.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-crystal-fire-33):153[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-True_Genius-34):145 Shive's invention sparked[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-Brittain1984p1695-35) Shockley's invention of the junction transistor.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-crystal-fire-33):143 A few months later he invented an entirely new, considerably more robust, type of transistor with a layer or 'sandwich' structure. This structure went on to be used for the vast majority of all transistors into the 1960s, and evolved into the bipolar junction transistor. Shockley later described the workings of the team as a "mixture of cooperation and competition". He also said that he kept some of his own work secret until his "hand was forced" by Shive's 1948 advance.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-:3-36) Shockley worked out a rather complete description of what he called the "sandwich" transistor, and a first [proof of principle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proof_of_concept "Proof of concept") was obtained on April 7, 1949.

Meanwhile, Shockley worked on his book, _[Electrons and Holes in Semiconductors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrons\_and\_Holes\_in\_Semiconductors "Electrons and Holes in Semiconductors")_, which was published as a 558-page treatise in 1950. The tome included Shockley's critical ideas of drift and diffusion and the differential equations that govern the flow of electrons in solid state crystals. [Shockley's diode equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shockley_diode_equation "Shockley diode equation") is also described. This seminal work became the reference text for other scientists working to develop and improve new variants of the transistor and other devices based on semiconductors.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-37)

This resulted in his invention of the [bipolar junction transistor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bipolar_junction_transistor "Bipolar junction transistor"), which was announced at a press conference on July 4, 1951.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-38)

The ensuing publicity generated by the "invention of the transistor" often thrust Shockley to the fore, much to the chagrin of Bardeen and Brattain. Bell Labs management, however, consistently presented all three inventors as a team. Though Shockley would correct the record where reporters gave him sole credit for the invention,[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-39) he eventually infuriated and alienated Bardeen and Brattain, and he essentially blocked the two from working on the junction transistor. Bardeen began pursuing a theory for superconductivity and left Bell Labs in 1951. Brattain refused to work with Shockley further and was assigned to another group. Neither Bardeen nor Brattain had much to do with the development of the transistor beyond the first year after its invention.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-40)

Shockley left Bell Labs around 1953 and took a job at Caltech.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-:4-41)

### Shockley Semiconductor

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=William_Shockley&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Shockley Semiconductor")]

Main article: [Shockley Semiconductor Laboratory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shockley_Semiconductor_Laboratory "Shockley Semiconductor Laboratory")

In 1956, Shockley started [Shockley Semiconductor Laboratory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shockley_Semiconductor_Laboratory "Shockley Semiconductor Laboratory") in [Mountain View, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mountain_View,_California "Mountain View, California"), which was close to his elderly mother in Palo Alto, California.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-42)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-43) The company, a division of [Beckman Instruments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beckman_Instruments "Beckman Instruments"), Inc., was the first establishment working on silicon semiconductor devices in what came to be known as [Silicon Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon_Valley "Silicon Valley").

Shockley recruited brilliant employees to his company, but alienated them by undermining them relentlessly.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-MM18-3)[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-:9-44) "He may have been the worst manager in the history of electronics", according to his biographer Joel Shurkin.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-:9-44)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-MM18-3) Shockley was autocratic, domineering, erratic, hard-to-please, and increasingly paranoid.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-45)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-:8-46) In one well-known incident, he demanded [lie detector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_detector "Lie detector") tests to find the "culprit" after a company secretary suffered a minor cut.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-:8-46) In late 1957, eight of Shockley's best researchers, who would come to be known as the "[traitorous eight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traitorous_eight "Traitorous eight")", resigned after Shockley decided not to continue research into silicon-based semiconductors;[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-Goodheart2006-47)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-:4-41) they went on to form [Fairchild Semiconductor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fairchild_Semiconductor "Fairchild Semiconductor"). Shockley Semiconductor never recovered from this loss.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-renamed_from_111_on_20260909164554-48) The company was purchased by [Clevite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clevite "Clevite") in 1960, sold again to [ITT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ITT_Corporation "ITT Corporation") in 1968, and shortly after, officially closed.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-renamed_from_111_on_20260909164554-48)

Over the course of the next 20 years, more than 65 new enterprises would end up having employee connections back to Fairchild.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-NetValley-49)

A group of about thirty colleagues have met on and off since 1956 to reminisce about their time with Shockley, "the man who brought silicon to Silicon Valley", as the group's organizer said in 2002.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-50)

## Racist and eugenicist views

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=William_Shockley&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Racist and eugenicist views")]

See also: [History of the race and intelligence controversy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_race_and_intelligence_controversy "History of the race and intelligence controversy")

After Shockley left his role as Director of Shockley Semiconductor in April 1960,[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-McLellan-51) he joined [Stanford University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University "Stanford University"), where he was appointed Alexander M. Poniatoff Professor of Engineering and Applied Science in 1963, a position he held until his retirement in 1975.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-52)

In the last two decades of his life, Shockley, who had no degree in [genetics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genetics "Genetics"), became widely known for his extreme views on [race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Race_(classification_of_human_beings) "Race (classification of human beings)") and [human intelligence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_intelligence "Human intelligence"), and his advocacy of [eugenics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eugenics "Eugenics").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-latimesobit-4)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-:6-7) As described by his _Los Angeles Times_ obituary, "He went from being a physicist with impeccable academic credentials to amateur geneticist, becoming a lightning rod whose views sparked campus demonstrations and a cascade of calumny." He thought his work was important to the future of humanity and he also described it as the most important aspect of his career. He argued that a higher rate of reproduction among purportedly less intelligent people was having a [dysgenic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dysgenics "Dysgenics") effect, and argued that a drop in average intelligence would lead to a decline in [civilization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civilization "Civilization"). He also claimed that [black people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_people "Black people") were genetically and intellectually inferior to [white people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_people "White people").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-latimesobit-4)

Shockley's biographer Joel Shurkin notes that for much of Shockley's life in the [racially segregated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racial_segregation_in_the_United_States "Racial segregation in the United States") United States of the time, he had almost no contact with black people.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-FOOTNOTEShurkin200652-53) Bo Lojek, a biographer and former colleague of Shockley, suggests that a 1963 local crime news story and shortly later a forwarded [J. P. Guilford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._P._Guilford "J. P. Guilford") article influenced Shockley's thinking.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-54)

Shockley was one of the [race theorists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scientific_racism "Scientific racism") who received money from the [Pioneer Fund](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pioneer_Fund "Pioneer Fund"), and at least one donation to him came from its founder, the eugenicist [Wickliffe Draper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wickliffe_Draper "Wickliffe Draper").[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-:2-55)[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-FOOTNOTEShurkin2006221%E2%80%93223-56) Shockley proposed that individuals with [IQs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IQ "IQ") below 100 should be paid to undergo voluntary [sterilization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sterilization_(medicine) "Sterilization (medicine)"), $1,000 for each of their IQ points under 100.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-latimesobit-4) This proposal led to the [University of Leeds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Leeds "University of Leeds") to withdraw its offer of an honorary degree to him.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-latimesobit-4) Anthropologist and far-right activist [Roger Pearson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Pearson_(anthropologist) "Roger Pearson (anthropologist)") defended Shockley in a self-published book co-authored with Shockley.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-57)

In 1973, [University of Wisconsin–Milwaukee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Wisconsin%E2%80%93Milwaukee "University of Wisconsin–Milwaukee") professor Edgar G. Epps argued that "William Shockley's position lends itself to racist interpretations".[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-:12-58) On _[Firing Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Firing\_Line\_(TV\_series) "Firing Line (TV series)")_ with [William F. Buckley Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_F._Buckley_Jr. "William F. Buckley Jr.") in 1974, Shockley argued, "My research leads me inescapably to the opinion that the major cause of the American Negro's intellectual and social deficits is hereditary and racially genetic in origin and, thus, not remediable to a major degree by practical improvements in the environment."[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-59)

[The Southern Poverty Law Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Poverty_Law_Center "Southern Poverty Law Center") describes Shockley as a [white nationalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_nationalism "White nationalism") who failed to produce evidence for his eugenic theories amidst "near-universal acknowledgement that his work was that of a racist crank".[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-:0-60) The science writer [Angela Saini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angela_Saini "Angela Saini") describes Shockley as having been "a notorious racist."[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-:2-55)

Shockley insisted that he was not a [racist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racism "Racism").[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-:12-58)[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-61) He wrote that his findings do not support [white supremacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_supremacy "White supremacy"), instead claiming that East Asians and Jews fare better than whites intellectually.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-:12-58) In 1973, Edgar Epps wrote that "I am pleased that Professor Shockley is not an Aryan supremacist, but I would remind him that a theory espousing hereditary superiority of Orientals or Jews is just as racist in nature as the Aryan supremacy doctrine".[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-:12-58)

Shockley's advocacy of eugenics triggered protests. In one incident, the science society [Sigma Xi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sigma_Xi "Sigma Xi"), fearing violence, canceled a 1968 convocation in [Brooklyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooklyn "Brooklyn") where Shockley was scheduled to speak.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-FOOTNOTEShurkin2006219%E2%80%93220-62)

In Atlanta in 1981, Shockley filed a [libel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Libel "Libel") suit against the _[Atlanta Constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta\_Constitution "Atlanta Constitution")_ after a science writer, [Roger Witherspoon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Witherspoon?action=edit&redlink=1 "Roger Witherspoon (page does not exist)"), compared Shockley's advocacy of a voluntary sterilization program to [Nazi human experimentation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazi_human_experimentation "Nazi human experimentation"). The suit took three years to go to trial. Shockley won the suit but he only received [one dollar in damages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Damages#Nominal_damages "Damages")[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-63) and he did not receive any [punitive damages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punitive_damages "Punitive damages"). Shockley's biographer Joel Shurkin, a science writer on the staff of Stanford University during those years, sums this statement up by saying that it was defamatory, but Shockley's reputation was not worth much by the time the trial reached a verdict.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-Shurkin2006pp259%E2%80%93260-64) Shockley taped his [telephone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telephone "Telephone") conversations with reporters, transcribed them, and sent the transcripts to the reporters by registered mail. At one point, he toyed with the idea of making the reporters take a simple quiz on his work before he would discuss the subject matter of it with them. His habit of saving all of his papers (including laundry lists) provides abundant documentation on his life for researchers.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-Shurkin2006p286-65)

Shockley was a candidate for the [Republican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States) "Republican Party (United States)") nomination in the [1982 United States Senate election in California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1982_United_States_Senate_election_in_California "1982 United States Senate election in California"). He ran on a [single-issue platform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Single-issue_politics "Single-issue politics") of opposing the "dysgenic threat" that he alleged [African-Americans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_Americans "African Americans") and other groups posed.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-66)[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-:0-60)[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-67) He came in eighth place in the primary, receiving 0.37% of the vote.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-68) According to Shurkin, by this time, "His racism destroyed his credibility. Almost no one wanted to be associated with him, and many of those who were willing did him more harm than good".[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-FOOTNOTEShurkin2006268-69)

### Foundation for Research and Education on Eugenics and Dysgenics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=William_Shockley&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Foundation for Research and Education on Eugenics and Dysgenics")]

The Foundation for Research and Education on Eugenics and Dysgenics (FREED) was a [non-profit organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nonprofit_organization "Nonprofit organization") founded in March 1970 in the United States formed to support the research of Shockley, who was the president of the foundation and [R. Travis Osborne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R._Travis_Osborne "R. Travis Osborne"), a member.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-70)[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-71)[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-Tucker_1994-72) The foundation released the newsletter "FREED" and research papers at [Stanford University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University "Stanford University").

The organization was founded according to its mission "solely for scientific and educational purposes related to human population and quality problems".[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-Tucker_1994-72)

From 1969 to 1976, the [Pioneer Fund](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pioneer_Fund "Pioneer Fund") allocated about $2.5 million ([adjusted-for-inflation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adjusted-for-inflation "Adjusted-for-inflation") in 2023) to support Shockley's endeavors. This funding was distributed through grants to [Stanford University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University "Stanford University") for the exploration of "research into the factors which affect genetic potential" and also directly to FREED.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-fighting-hate/extremist-73)[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-74)

Via FREED, Shockley promoted his concept of a "Voluntary Sterilization Bonus Plan", proposing to compensate [economically disadvantaged](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economically_disadvantaged "Economically disadvantaged") women for undergoing [sterilization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sterilization_(medicine) "Sterilization (medicine)") procedures.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-fighting-hate/extremist-73)

In 1970, Shockley listed former [senator of Alaska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_United_States_senators_from_Alaska "List of United States senators from Alaska")[Ernest Gruening](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernest_Gruening "Ernest Gruening") as a director of FREED.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-75)

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=William_Shockley&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Personal life")]

At age 23 and while still a student, Shockley married Jean Bailey in August 1933. The couple had two sons and a daughter.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-76) Shockley separated from her in 1953.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-:4-41) He married Emily Lanning, a psychiatric nurse, in 1955; she helped him with some of his theories.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-:4-41)[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-77) Although one of his sons earned a PhD at Stanford University and his daughter graduated from Radcliffe College, Shockley believed his children "represent a very significant regression ... my first wife – their mother – had not as high an academic-achievement standing as I had".[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-latimesobit-4)

Shockley was an accomplished rock climber, going often to the [Shawangunks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shawangunk_Ridge "Shawangunk Ridge") in the [Hudson River Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson_Valley "Hudson Valley"). His 1953 route known as "Shockley's Ceiling", is one of the classic climbing routes in the area.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-Crystal_Fire_p._132-29)[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-78)[Mountain Project](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mountain_Project "Mountain Project"), a web-based [climbing guidebook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climbing_guidebook "Climbing guidebook"), reports that the route's name has been changed to "The Ceiling" due to Shockley's eugenics controversies.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-79) A 1996 guidebook notes that the original party on this route avoided the ceiling in question. The guidebook lists this variation as "Shockley's Without." He was popular as a speaker, lecturer, and amateur magician. He once "magically" produced a bouquet of roses at the end of his address before the [American Physical Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Physical_Society "American Physical Society").

Shockley was also known in his early years for elaborate practical jokes.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-80) He had a longtime hobby of [raising ant colonies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ant-keeping "Ant-keeping").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-:1-15)

Shockley [donated sperm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donated_sperm "Donated sperm") to the [Repository for Germinal Choice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Repository_for_Germinal_Choice "Repository for Germinal Choice"), a [sperm bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sperm_bank "Sperm bank") founded by [Robert Klark Graham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Klark_Graham "Robert Klark Graham") in hopes of spreading humanity's best [genes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gene "Gene"). The bank, called by the media the "Nobel Prize sperm bank", claimed to have three Nobel Prize-winning donors, though Shockley was the only one to publicly acknowledge his involvement.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-81) However, Shockley's controversial views brought the Repository for Germinal Choice a degree of notoriety and may have discouraged other Nobel Prize winners from donating sperm.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-82)

Shockley was unhappy in his life and was often [psychologically](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychological_abuse "Psychological abuse") and sometimes [physically abusive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physical_abuse "Physical abuse") toward his sons.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-83) On one occasion, he reportedly played [Russian roulette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_roulette "Russian roulette") on himself as part of a [suicide attempt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suicide_attempt "Suicide attempt").[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-:4-41)[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-84)

Shockley died of [prostate cancer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prostate_cancer "Prostate cancer") on August 12, 1989, in [Stanford, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford,_California "Stanford, California"), at the age of 79.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-obit-85) At the time of his death he was estranged from most of his friends and family, with the exception of his second wife. His children learned of his death by reading his obituary in the newspaper.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bradford_Shockley#cite_note-86) He is buried in [Alta Mesa Memorial Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alta_Mesa_Memorial_Park "Alta Mesa Memorial Park") in Palo Alto, California.
